payload.rationale: The August 2026 U-3 rate was 4.1%. For the October reading (released ~Nov 6) to resolve YES, it must print 4.4% or higher, a rise of at least 0.3 percentage points over two survey months. Historically, monthly changes in the unemployment rate are small (typically ±0.1pp, standard deviation roughly 0.1–0.15pp), and two-month rises of 0.3pp or more from a stable level occur infrequently outside of clear labor-market deterioration. The September FOMC median for Q4 unemployment is 4.1%, indicating policymakers expected stability, not a sharp rise. Reasons the estimate could be too low: payroll growth was very weak in June and July (31k and 21k after revisions), and the August 162k print could be revised down or prove an outlier; a labor market adding jobs below breakeven can push unemployment up quickly, and household-survey noise occasionally produces 0.2pp jumps in a single month. Elevated inflation (PCE 3.7%) limits Fed easing, adding downside risk to labor demand. Reasons it could be too high: the Fed's central projection and the August rebound suggest the labor market is stable around 4.1%; reaching 4.4% would require two consecutive adverse moves or one unusually large jump, and low labor-force participation dynamics have kept the rate contained. Balancing base rates against modest downside risk signals, I estimate roughly a 10% chance.
limitations: September and October data are unknown; only three payroll readings and one unemployment print are supplied.
The FOMC Q4 median is a quarterly average and a forecast, not an October observation.
No fitted statistical model; base rates for two-month unemployment changes are drawn from general background knowledge.
Household-survey sampling noise and possible revisions add irreducible uncertainty.
